Technical Details

1. Model Framework

1.1 Longitudinal Sub-Model

Observed biomarker measurements for subject ii at time TijT_{ij}:

Vij=mi(Tij)+εij,εij∼𝒩(0,σe2),i=1,…,n,j=1,…,niV_{ij} = m_i(T_{ij}) + \varepsilon_{ij}, \quad \varepsilon_{ij} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_e^2), \quad i = 1,\ldots,n, \quad j = 1,\ldots,n_i

The true trajectory mi(t)m_i(t) satisfies a second-order linear ODE:

m̈i(t)+2ξiωiṁi(t)+ωi2mi(t)=fi(t)\ddot{m}_i(t) + 2\xi_i\omega_i\,\dot{m}_i(t) + \omega_i^2\,m_i(t) = f_i(t)

with initial conditions mi(0)=m0,im_i(0) = m_{0,i} and ṁi(0)=v0,i\dot{m}_i(0) = v_{0,i}, where:

  • ωi>0\omega_i > 0: natural frequency (controls oscillation speed)
  • ξi>0\xi_i > 0: damping ratio (ξ<1\xi < 1: underdamped oscillation; ξ>1\xi > 1: overdamped monotonic decay; ξ=1\xi = 1: critical damping)
  • fi(t)=𝜷X⊤𝑿i(t)f_i(t) = \boldsymbol{\beta}_X^\top \mathbf{X}_i(t): covariate-driven forcing

1.2 Parameterization and Random Effects

Rewriting as m̈i(t)=b1,imi(t)+b2,iṁi(t)+fi(t)\ddot{m}_i(t) = b_{1,i}\,m_i(t) + b_{2,i}\,\dot{m}_i(t) + f_i(t), the ODE coefficients are:

b1,i=−ωi2,b2,i=−2ξiωib_{1,i} = -\omega_i^2, \quad b_{2,i} = -2\xi_i\omega_i

Stability requires b1,i<0b_{1,i} < 0 and b2,i<0b_{2,i} < 0 (both eigenvalues of the characteristic equation have negative real parts). This is enforced through a log parameterization with multiplicative random effects:

b1,i=−exp⁡(θ1+u1,i),b2,i=−exp⁡(θ2+u2,i)b_{1,i} = -\exp(\theta_1 + u_{1,i}), \quad b_{2,i} = -\exp(\theta_2 + u_{2,i})

where θ1=log⁡(ω2)\theta_1 = \log(\omega^2) and θ2=log⁡(2ξω)\theta_2 = \log(2\xi\omega) are population-level parameters, and u1,i,u2,iu_{1,i}, u_{2,i} are zero-mean random effects. Since exp⁡(⋅)>0\exp(\cdot) > 0, we have b1,i<0b_{1,i} < 0 and b2,i<0b_{2,i} < 0 for all subjects regardless of random effect values. The multiplicative structure preserves the sign while allowing subject-specific variation: ωi2=ω2eu1,i\omega_i^2 = \omega^2 e^{u_{1,i}}.

The complete random effects vector for subject ii is:

𝒃i=(m0,i−m‾0v0,i−v‾0u1,iu2,i⋮)∼𝒩(𝟎,𝚺b)\mathbf{b}_i = \begin{pmatrix} m_{0,i} - \bar{m}_0 \\ v_{0,i} - \bar{v}_0 \\ u_{1,i} \\ u_{2,i} \\ \vdots \end{pmatrix} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_b)

where the first two components capture initial-state heterogeneity (additive), followed by dynamics RE (multiplicative on log scale), and optional forcing RE.

1.3 Survival Sub-Model

The hazard function links the biomarker trajectory to event risk:

λi(t)=λ0(t)exp⁡[αvaluemi(t)+αvelocityṁiγ(t)+𝑾i⊤𝝓]\lambda_i(t) = \lambda_0(t)\,\exp\!\left[\alpha_\text{value}\,m_i(t) + \alpha_\text{velocity}\,\dot{m}_i^\gamma(t) + \mathbf{W}_i^\top\boldsymbol{\phi}\right]

where:

  • λ0(t)=exp⁡[𝜼⊤𝑩(t)]\lambda_0(t) = \exp[\boldsymbol{\eta}^\top\mathbf{B}(t)]: B-spline baseline hazard with basis 𝑩(t)\mathbf{B}(t) and coefficients 𝜼\boldsymbol{\eta}
  • γ∈{0,1,2}\gamma \in \{0, 1, 2\}: velocity power (0 = value only, 1 = linear velocity, 2 = quadratic velocity)
  • 𝑾i\mathbf{W}_i: baseline covariates with coefficients 𝝓\boldsymbol{\phi}

The cumulative hazard Λi(t)=∫0tλi(s)ds\Lambda_i(t) = \int_0^t \lambda_i(s)\,ds is computed via composite Simpson’s rule.

1.4 Joint Likelihood

Assuming conditional independence of the longitudinal and survival processes given 𝒃i\mathbf{b}_i, the joint likelihood for subject ii is:

Li(𝜽)=∫p(𝑽i∣𝒃i)⏟longitudinal⋅p(Ti,δi∣𝒃i)⏟survival⋅p(𝒃i)⏟priord𝒃iL_i(\boldsymbol{\theta}) = \int \underbrace{p(\mathbf{V}_i \mid \mathbf{b}_i)}_{\text{longitudinal}} \cdot \underbrace{p(T_i, \delta_i \mid \mathbf{b}_i)}_{\text{survival}} \cdot \underbrace{p(\mathbf{b}_i)}_{\text{prior}}\,d\mathbf{b}_i

with components:

p(𝑽i∣𝒃i)=∏j=1niϕ(Vij;mi(Tij∣𝒃i),σe2)p(Ti,δi∣𝒃i)=λi(Ti∣𝒃i)δiexp⁡[−Λi(Ti∣𝒃i)]p(𝒃i)=𝒩(𝟎,𝚺b)\begin{aligned} p(\mathbf{V}_i \mid \mathbf{b}_i) &= \prod_{j=1}^{n_i} \phi\!\left(V_{ij};\, m_i(T_{ij} \mid \mathbf{b}_i),\, \sigma_e^2\right) \\ p(T_i, \delta_i \mid \mathbf{b}_i) &= \lambda_i(T_i \mid \mathbf{b}_i)^{\delta_i}\,\exp\!\left[-\Lambda_i(T_i \mid \mathbf{b}_i)\right] \\ p(\mathbf{b}_i) &= \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_b) \end{aligned}

where 𝜽\boldsymbol{\theta} collects all fixed parameters: (𝜼,αvalue,αvelocity,𝝓,θ1,θ2,𝜷X,m‾0,v‾0,σe,vech(𝚺b))(\boldsymbol{\eta}, \alpha_\text{value}, \alpha_\text{velocity}, \boldsymbol{\phi}, \theta_1, \theta_2, \boldsymbol{\beta}_X, \bar{m}_0, \bar{v}_0, \sigma_e, \text{vech}(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_b)).

2. ODE Solver

2.1 Exact Solution via Cayley–Hamilton

The ODE m̈=b1m+b2ṁ+f\ddot{m} = b_1 m + b_2 \dot{m} + f with constant forcing over [t,t+Δt][t, t{+}\Delta t] has the exact solution:

(m(t+Δt)ṁ(t+Δt))=exp⁡(AΔt)(m(t)ṁ(t))+∫0Δtexp⁡(As)ds(0f)\begin{pmatrix} m(t{+}\Delta t) \\ \dot{m}(t{+}\Delta t) \end{pmatrix} = \exp(A\Delta t) \begin{pmatrix} m(t) \\ \dot{m}(t) \end{pmatrix} + \int_0^{\Delta t} \exp(As)\,ds \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ f \end{pmatrix}

where A=(01b1b2)A = \bigl(\begin{smallmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ b_1 & b_2 \end{smallmatrix}\bigr) is the companion matrix. By the Cayley–Hamilton theorem, for any 2×22 \times 2 matrix AA with characteristic polynomial λ2−b2λ−b1=0\lambda^2 - b_2\lambda - b_1 = 0, the matrix exponential can be written as exp⁡(AΔt)=a0I+a1A\exp(A\Delta t) = a_0 I + a_1 A for scalar coefficients a0,a1a_0, a_1. Expanding:

(m(t+Δt)ṁ(t+Δt))=(a0a1b1a1a0+b2a1)(m(t)ṁ(t))+f(J1a1)\begin{pmatrix} m(t{+}\Delta t) \\ \dot{m}(t{+}\Delta t) \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} a_0 & a_1 \\ b_1 a_1 & a_0 + b_2 a_1 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} m(t) \\ \dot{m}(t) \end{pmatrix} + f \begin{pmatrix} J_1 \\ a_1 \end{pmatrix}

The forcing integrals are derived from the augmented 3×33 \times 3 system with state (m,ṁ,f)⊤(m, \dot{m}, f)^\top: the position forcing integral is J1=(a0−1)/b1J_1 = (a_0 - 1)/b_1, and the velocity forcing term is simply f⋅a1f \cdot a_1 (which can also be verified by differentiating the position solution).

The coefficients a0,a1a_0, a_1 depend on the eigenvalue structure. Let μ=b2Δt/2\mu = b_2\Delta t/2 (half-trace), D=b22+4b1D = b_2^2 + 4b_1 (discriminant), and s2=DΔt2/4s^2 = D\Delta t^2/4:

Underdamped (D<0D < 0, ξ<1\xi < 1): complex eigenvalues with damped frequency ωd=−s2\omega_d = \sqrt{-s^2}.

a0=eμ(cos⁡ωd−μsinc(ωd)),a1=eμΔtsinc(ωd)a_0 = e^{\mu}(\cos\omega_d - \mu\,\text{sinc}(\omega_d)), \quad a_1 = e^{\mu}\Delta t\,\text{sinc}(\omega_d)

where sinc(x)=sin⁡(x)/x\text{sinc}(x) = \sin(x)/x.

Overdamped (D>0D > 0, ξ>1\xi > 1): two distinct real eigenvalues with δ=s2\delta = \sqrt{s^2}.

a0=eμ(cosh⁡δ−μsinhc(δ)),a1=eμΔtsinhc(δ)a_0 = e^{\mu}(\cosh\delta - \mu\,\text{sinhc}(\delta)), \quad a_1 = e^{\mu}\Delta t\,\text{sinhc}(\delta)

where sinhc(x)=sinh⁡(x)/x\text{sinhc}(x) = \sinh(x)/x.

Critically damped (D=0D = 0, ξ=1\xi = 1): repeated eigenvalue.

a0=eμ(1−μ),a1=eμΔta_0 = e^{\mu}(1 - \mu), \quad a_1 = e^{\mu}\Delta t

2.2 Numerical Stability for Automatic Differentiation

The exact formulas above are mathematically equivalent but present numerical challenges for gradient-based optimization with automatic differentiation (AD):

  1. Branch discontinuity at D=0D = 0: The transition between sin⁡/cos\sin/\cos and sinh⁡/cosh\sinh/\cosh branches involves |D|\sqrt{|D|}, whose derivative ddD|D|→∞\frac{d}{dD}\sqrt{|D|} \to \infty as D→0D \to 0. During optimization, random effects can push individual DiD_i across zero, creating gradient spikes that destabilize Newton’s method.

  2. Division by zero: sinc(x)=sin⁡(x)/x\text{sinc}(x) = \sin(x)/x and sinhc(x)=sinh⁡(x)/x\text{sinhc}(x) = \sinh(x)/x are removable singularities at x=0x = 0, but naive evaluation produces 0/00/0.

  3. AD tape evaluation: AD frameworks evaluate both branches of a conditional expression during the forward pass (selecting the result via a smooth switch). The non-selected branch must remain finite to avoid corrupting gradients.

The implementation addresses these via a three-way conditional in s2s^2:

Taylor branch (|s2|<ϵ|s^2| < \epsilon): Bypasses ⋅\sqrt{\cdot} entirely using the unified Taylor expansion. Since sinc(ix)=sinhc(x)\text{sinc}(ix) = \text{sinhc}(x) (because sin⁡(ix)/(ix)=sinh⁡(x)/x\sin(ix)/(ix) = \sinh(x)/x), both branches share the same series in s2s^2:

Sc≈1+s26+s4120,Cc≈1+s22+s424\text{Sc} \approx 1 + \frac{s^2}{6} + \frac{s^4}{120}, \quad \text{Cc} \approx 1 + \frac{s^2}{2} + \frac{s^4}{24}

Direct branches (|s2|≥ϵ|s^2| \geq \epsilon): The sinhc\text{sinhc} and sinc\text{sinc} functions guard against 0/00/0 by replacing the denominator with 11 when |x|<ϵ′|x| < \epsilon', so the non-selected branch evaluates to a finite value with finite gradient.

Forcing integral singularity: J1=(a0−1)/b1J_1 = (a_0 - 1)/b_1 has a removable singularity at b1=0b_1 = 0. The limit lim⁡b1→0J1=Δt2expm1c2(b2Δt)\lim_{b_1 \to 0} J_1 = \Delta t^2\,\text{expm1c2}(b_2\Delta t) where expm1c2(x)=(ex−1−x)/x2\text{expm1c2}(x) = (e^x - 1 - x)/x^2 is used as a Taylor fallback.

2.3 Physical Stability Guarantee

The log parameterization b1=−exp⁡(θ1)b_1 = -\exp(\theta_1), b2=−exp⁡(θ2)b_2 = -\exp(\theta_2) ensures b1<0b_1 < 0 and b2<0b_2 < 0 for all parameter values. This provides:

  • Bounded trajectories: Both eigenvalues have negative real parts (underdamped: Re(λ)=b2/2<0\text{Re}(\lambda) = b_2/2 < 0; overdamped: λ1,2<0\lambda_{1,2} < 0 since D<|b2|\sqrt{D} < |b_2|), so trajectories decay rather than grow. The factor eμ=eb2Δt/2<1e^\mu = e^{b_2\Delta t/2} < 1 prevents overflow in the matrix exponential.
  • Convex inner optimization: With stable dynamics, the negative log-likelihood as a function of random effects is unimodal, ensuring the Laplace approximation (Section 3) is valid.
  • Well-conditioned Hessian: The inner Hessian eigenvalues remain bounded, enabling fast Newton convergence for the random effects mode.

3. Parameter Estimation

3.1 Laplace Approximation

The marginal log-likelihood ℓ(𝜽)=∑i=1nlog⁡Li(𝜽)\ell(\boldsymbol{\theta}) = \sum_{i=1}^n \log L_i(\boldsymbol{\theta}) is intractable due to the random effects integral. We use the Laplace approximation:

log⁡Li(𝜽)≈gi(𝜽,𝒃̂i)+12log⁡|2π𝑯i−1|\log L_i(\boldsymbol{\theta}) \approx g_i(\boldsymbol{\theta},\, \hat{\mathbf{b}}_i) + \frac{1}{2}\log\!\left|2\pi\,\mathbf{H}_i^{-1}\right|

where gi(𝜽,𝒃)=log⁡[p(𝑽i,Ti,δi∣𝒃)p(𝒃)]g_i(\boldsymbol{\theta}, \mathbf{b}) = \log\!\left[p(\mathbf{V}_i, T_i, \delta_i \mid \mathbf{b})\, p(\mathbf{b})\right] is the joint log-density, 𝒃̂i=arg⁡max⁡𝒃gi(𝜽,𝒃)\hat{\mathbf{b}}_i = \arg\max_{\mathbf{b}} g_i(\boldsymbol{\theta}, \mathbf{b}) is the posterior mode, and 𝑯i=−∇𝒃2gi|𝒃̂i\mathbf{H}_i = -\nabla^2_{\mathbf{b}} g_i\big|_{\hat{\mathbf{b}}_i} is the negative Hessian.

3.2 Optimization

Estimation proceeds as a nested optimization:

  1. Inner problem: For given 𝜽\boldsymbol{\theta}, find the posterior modes 𝒃̂i(𝜽)\hat{\mathbf{b}}_i(\boldsymbol{\theta}) via Newton’s method
  2. Outer problem: Maximize the Laplace-approximated marginal log-likelihood over 𝜽\boldsymbol{\theta}

The gradient of the outer objective is computed via the implicit function theorem: since ∇𝒃gi=𝟎\nabla_{\mathbf{b}} g_i = \mathbf{0} at 𝒃̂i\hat{\mathbf{b}}_i, the derivative d𝒃̂i/d𝜽d\hat{\mathbf{b}}_i/d\boldsymbol{\theta} does not need to be computed explicitly. Automatic differentiation provides exact gradients through both the log-determinant correction and the joint log-density.

3.3 Standard Errors

The observed information matrix is obtained from the Hessian of the Laplace-approximated marginal log-likelihood. Standard errors for fixed effects 𝜽\boldsymbol{\theta} are:

SE(θ̂k)=[ℐ(𝜽̂)−1]kk\text{SE}(\hat{\theta}_k) = \sqrt{[\mathcal{I}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}})^{-1}]_{kk}}

3.4 Warm Start Strategy

For models with dynamics random effects, a two-phase approach improves convergence:

  1. Phase 1: Fit a reduced model without dynamics RE (only initial-state RE). This converges quickly because the inner optimization is low-dimensional.
  2. Phase 2: Use Phase 1 estimates as starting values for the full model. The inner Newton starts near the mode, accelerating convergence.

For the joint model, MarginalODE (longitudinal only) provides initial values, followed by time-dependent Cox regression for survival parameters.

4. Derived Physical Parameters

4.1 Point Estimates

From the estimated log-scale parameters θ̂1\hat\theta_1 and θ̂2\hat\theta_2:

ω̂=exp⁡(θ̂1/2),ξ̂=12exp⁡(θ̂2−θ̂1/2)\hat\omega = \exp(\hat\theta_1 / 2), \quad \hat\xi = \frac{1}{2}\exp(\hat\theta_2 - \hat\theta_1/2)

The natural period is T̂=2π/ω̂\hat{T} = 2\pi/\hat\omega.

4.2 Standard Errors via Delta Method

Let 𝑽=Var(θ̂1,θ̂2)\mathbf{V} = \text{Var}(\hat\theta_1, \hat\theta_2) be the estimated covariance from the information matrix.

Natural frequency:

∂ω∂θ1=ω2,SE(ω̂)=ω̂2V11\frac{\partial\omega}{\partial\theta_1} = \frac{\omega}{2}, \quad \text{SE}(\hat\omega) = \frac{\hat\omega}{2}\sqrt{V_{11}}

Damping ratio:

∂ξ∂θ1=−ξ2,∂ξ∂θ2=ξ\frac{\partial\xi}{\partial\theta_1} = -\frac{\xi}{2}, \quad \frac{\partial\xi}{\partial\theta_2} = \xi

Var(ξ̂)=ξ̂24V11+ξ̂2V22−ξ̂2V12\text{Var}(\hat\xi) = \frac{\hat\xi^2}{4}V_{11} + \hat\xi^2 V_{22} - \hat\xi^2 V_{12}

5. Computational Details

5.1 Hazard Integration

The cumulative hazard Λi(Ti)=∫0Tiλi(t)dt\Lambda_i(T_i) = \int_0^{T_i}\lambda_i(t)\,dt is approximated via composite Simpson’s rule. Each observation interval [tk,tk+1][t_k, t_{k+1}] is subdivided into QQ quadrature sub-intervals, with the ODE solved at midpoints and endpoints:

∫tktk+1λi(t)dt≈∑q=1QΔtq6[λi(L)+4λi(M)+λi(R)]\int_{t_k}^{t_{k+1}} \lambda_i(t)\,dt \approx \sum_{q=1}^{Q} \frac{\Delta t_q}{6}\!\left[\lambda_i^{(L)} + 4\lambda_i^{(M)} + \lambda_i^{(R)}\right]

5.2 Covariance Structure

The random effects covariance 𝚺b\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_b is parameterized via the log-Cholesky decomposition: 𝚺b=DRD\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_b = D\,R\,D where D=diag(exp⁡(𝝈))D = \text{diag}(\exp(\boldsymbol{\sigma})) and RR is a correlation matrix from an unconstrained vector. This ensures positive-definiteness.

5.3 Parallel Computation

The log-likelihood decomposes as ℓ(𝜽)=∑i=1nℓi(𝜽)\ell(\boldsymbol{\theta}) = \sum_{i=1}^n \ell_i(\boldsymbol{\theta}), where each subject’s contribution is independent. This is parallelized across subjects.
